title: Refining Prompts for Better Outputs
summary: Students learn a refinement loop - set the goal, judge the output, name one weakness, make a single targeted change, and re-judge - so they can say exactly why a prompt change improved the result.
objectives: Improve a weak prompt so the output better meets the goal.
Explain which change improved the output and why it worked.

body: You ask an AI to 'write about Al Ain' and get a dull, general paragraph. Was the AI wrong - or was the prompt?
Today you become a prompt engineer who sets a clear goal, judges the output against it, and makes one smart change at a time. Best of all, you will be able to say exactly why your change worked.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can turn a weak prompt into a stronger one that better meets the goal.
I can name the exact change I made and explain why it improved the output.
I can judge an output against the goal instead of just accepting it.

terms.definition: The instruction and context you give an AI to guide its output.
What you want the output to achieve, stated clearly.
A limit you set, such as length, tone, or format.
Unclear or open to more than one meaning.
Goal, judge, name the weakness, change, re-judge - repeated.

sections.heading: Judge before you change
body: You cannot improve an output until you judge it honestly against the [[goal]]. Ask: what is missing, and what is off-target?
Common weaknesses in a prompt are a missing audience, missing format, missing [[constraint]], or an [[ambiguous]] task. Naming the weakness tells you exactly what to fix.

sections.heading: Change one thing, and know why
body: Strong refiners change **one thing at a time** and predict why it should help before they test it. That way, when the output improves, they know which change did it.
Specificity comes from the task, the audience, and the format - never from personal or private information. A precise [[prompt]] is not a personal one.

sections.label: Refining is a loop, not a line
sections.heading: Judge, change one thing, judge again
sections.altText: A loop: judge the output you got, change one thing about the prompt, run it again, then judge whether that change helped.
sections.repeatLabel: not good enough yet — go round again
sections.caption: A prompt is rarely right first time, and that is normal. **Keeping the receipts — which change, what happened — is what turns guessing into refining.**

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will take a weak prompt with a clear goal, name one weakness, write a targeted v2, predict its effect, and check against the revealed output.
items: Read the weak prompt and its goal.
Judge the v1 output and name one weakness.
Write a v2 that targets only that weakness.
Predict how the output should change and why.
Compare with the revealed v2 output and log it.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Why is changing one thing at a time smarter than changing many?
How can you make a prompt specific without adding any private information?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one change that most improved your output and why it worked.
Describe a time a clearer instruction would have helped you get a better result in real life.

worksheet.title: Week 2 - Core - Worksheet | Refining Prompts for Better Outputs

questions.prompt: For the weak prompt given, name one weakness and write a v2 that targets only that weakness.
questions.stem:
The weakness is ___.
My v2 prompt is ___.
questions.lookFor: Names a weakness that genuinely matches the output problem (ambiguous task, or missing audience, format, or constraint), and a v2 that directly targets that one named weakness rather than bundling several edits or simply lengthening the prompt.

questions.prompt: After the reveal, explain the causal reason your change improved the output.
questions.stem:
My change was ___.
It improved the output because ___.
questions.lookFor: A causal explanation linking the specific change to the improvement (e.g. naming the audience and length removed the model's need to guess, so the output became focused and age-appropriate). Reward causal reasoning, not 'it is better'.

questions.prompt: Record your v1, the weakness, your v2 change, the predicted effect, and the observed effect.
questions.stem: v1 prompt | Weakness named | v2 change | Predicted vs observed effect
questions.lookFor: A usable log in which one change is recorded per row with a stated reason, so the improvement can be attributed to a cause; predicted and observed effects are both recorded and compared, not just asserted.

questions.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences which prompt change improved your output and the reason it worked.
questions.lookFor: Names one specific change and gives a clear causal reason for the improvement. Partial: a general reason with a weak causal link. Not yet: states it is better with no reason.

questions.prompt: Write a v3 that improves the output on a second goal (for example, making it both clearer and more accurate) without losing the first improvement.
questions.lookFor: A v3 that adds a gain on a second dimension while preserving the first gain, with reasoning that shows awareness that the two goals must both be met rather than traded away.

formative.targets: Grade 5 Advanced: refines prompts to improve output quality and explains why
formative.check: Prompt-refinement log: v1 to v2 with a reasoned justification
formative.successCriteria: Makes a refinement that measurably improves the output and explains the causal reason.
